text: Jordan is two hours into the Friday overnight shift at Thornfield Financial Services' SOC, running the 24x7 rotation from Chapter 1. Three alerts land in the queue within ten minutes of each other, and all three involve a login or an account doing something slightly unusual. None of them announce whether they're a false positive or a real incident - that's exactly what Chapter 5's validate, scope, and classify process is built to work out.

Alert A flags repeated failed logins on the nightly backup service account. Alert B flags a new-country login for the Director of Sales. Alert C flags the same kind of new-location login for an accounts-payable clerk, paired with a mailbox rule change. All three start the same way. None of them end up classified the same way.

Alert A's failed logons, forwarded through Windows Event Forwarding, are real events. Scoping them against the change calendar turns up a password-rotation ticket that closed 22 minutes before the first failure - the backup job's stored credential just hadn't synced yet. That's a false positive with a documented root cause, closed with a case note referencing the ticket number.

Alert B's login from Lisbon succeeded with MFA approved on a registered device, so there's no sign of a stolen credential. Scoping it against the travel request system confirms an approved conference trip starting that morning, with no mailbox changes or download spikes anywhere on the account. The alert correctly caught a real new-location login - it's a true positive, just a benign one - closed with a short travel exception.

Alert C looks the same at first glance, until scoping tells a very different story. The same account logs in from Chicago, then from Hanoi 39 minutes later - physically impossible travel - with the second login authenticating over a legacy protocol that skips MFA entirely. Minutes later, a hidden inbox rule appears, forwarding every invoice and wire-transfer email to an external address. Chapter 4's correlation logic is what ties the login anomaly and the mailbox change into one alert. This meets every one of Chapter 5's escalation criteria at once, so Jordan writes a full case note and hands it straight to Tier 2.
Three alerts, three different verdicts, from the same triage process every time. Next up: building the exact correlation rule that caught Alert C's impossible travel in the first place.
